details.expected: Requirements. Municipalities can introduce environmental zones under the national framework. Class 1 concerns heavy buses and heavy goods vehicles; class 2 concerns passenger cars and light buses/goods vehicles. For class 2, spark-ignition vehicles need Euro 5 or Euro 6 and diesel vehicles need Euro 6. For light vehicles, class 3 ordinarily permits only electric, fuel-cell or qualifying gas vehicles; gas vehicles must meet the specified Euro 6 emissions criteria. expected_segments: Calculate journey consumption and savings

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-011 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Fuel arithmetic · Understand the unit. A consumption rate of 6.5 litres per 100 km means 6.5 litres for each 100 km under the supplied or measured conditions. A 200 km journey at the same assumed rate uses twice as much, while 50 km uses half as much. Actual consumption varies with vehicle, load, road, weather and driving. Transportstyrelsen: economical driving supplies the driving context; the equations below are editorial arithmetic derived from the unit, not agency-prescribed formulas.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-012 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Journey consumption: journey litres = distance in km × consumption in litres/100 km ÷ 100. Divide distance by 100 to find the number of 100 km portions, then multiply by the supplied rate. The kilometres cancel, leaving litres. Retain decimal working and round only the final result at the precision requested.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-013 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Consumption example · 120 km at 6.5 litres/100 km. The journey contains 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 portions of 100 km. Consumption = 1.2 × 6.5 = 7.8 litres. Do not multiply distance by the rate without dividing by 100; that would misread the unit.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-014 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Savings from a supplied reduction: litres saved = distance in km × reduction in litres/100 km ÷ 100. If two consumption rates are supplied, subtract the lower rate from the higher first. Multiply that difference by the number of 100 km portions. A supplied saving is an exercise assumption, not a guaranteed benefit of a particular driving technique.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-015 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Savings example · A reduction of 1.5 litres/100 km over 300 km. The journey has 300 ÷ 100 = 3 portions. Savings = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 litres. This is the difference in litres used, not the new total consumption. You need the original or new consumption rate to calculate either total.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-016 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Two-rate example · 7.0 and 6.5 litres/100 km over 240 km. First find the rate difference: 7.0 − 6.5 = 0.5 litres/100 km. Savings = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.2 litres. The original journey uses 16.8 litres and the lower-rate journey 15.6 litres; their difference is also 1.2 litres. No percentage-saving promise is implied.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-017 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Precision and midpoint rounding · Keep the exact result visible. Some supplied savings exercises display one-decimal answers without specifying precision or a rounding convention in their prompts. Four such examples below use ties-to-even for the displayed keyed value. This rounds to the nearest tenth; at an exact halfway value, choose the tenth whose retained digit is even. It differs from rounding a halfway value upwards. Do not call a rounded value the exact amount, or silently apply one convention where another is intended.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-018 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Four midpoint examples. A reduction of 0.5 litres/100 km over 150 km gives exactly 0.75 litres, displayed as 0.8 to one decimal using ties-to-even. A reduction of 1.5 over 150 km gives exactly 2.25 litres, displayed as 2.2. A reduction of 0.5 over 250 km gives exactly 1.25 litres, displayed as 1.2. A reduction of 1.5 over 250 km gives exactly 3.75 litres, displayed as 3.8. The units for every reduction are litres/100 km.

checks.name: M09-L02/teaching-019 reader content and answer reveal

expected_segments: Compare conventions. With ordinary half-up rounding to one decimal, 2.25 becomes 2.3 and 1.25 becomes 1.3; ties-to-even gives 2.2 and 1.2. The exact products remain 2.25 and 1.25 litres. For these supplied examples, keep the exact arithmetic and the disclosed displayed-answer convention separate. For a new problem, follow its stated precision/convention; if they are absent, report the exact result and recognise that a rounded answer needs an assumption. Round once at the end, not the rate or intermediate product.

expected_segments: Try the fuel arithmetic. (A) Find journey consumption for 80 km at 6.5 litres/100 km.
